newsitem.title: BAHAMAS: Hurricane Lili spares Bermuda, Bahamas clean up.
newsitem.headline: Hurricane Lili spares Bermuda, Bahamas clean up.

text.p: Crews worked to restore power to the battered islands of the central Bahamas on Sunday as Hurricane Lili swept past Bermuda, sparing the British colony.

Heavy rain pelted the island but the center of the storm remained far enough offshore that Bermuda officials did not consider it a threat and did not gear up the emergency center or advise residents to batten down.

At 5 p.m. EDT (2100 GMT), the center of Lili was located at latitude 30.9 north, longitude 62.5 west, about 155 miles (250 km) southeast of Bermuda, and moving northeast at 24 mph (39 kph), the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami said.
Its maximum winds had decreased to 85 mph (135 kph) and additional weakening was expected in the next 24 hours, forecasters said.

Lili appeared to be fading after a damaging rampage that began last week off the coast of Central America. Flooding from the storm was blamed for 10 deaths in Nicaragua, Honduras and Costa Rica before it moved north over Cuba and then east through the central Bahamas.

Bahamas government officials on Sunday toured the hard-hit islands of San Salvador, Great Exuma and Long Island, where Lili ripped roofs off dozens of homes, flooded streets and damaged banana crops, the Bahamas Broadcasting Corp. reported.
No casualties were reported, but electricity to many parts of the islands was cut and emergency crews were working to repair toppled poles and shredded lines.

On San Salvador, a 25-mile long (40 km) island, power was out to three-quarters of the 1,000 residents. But Commissioner Charles King, the government representative on the island, said San Salvador had otherwise weathered the storm well.

"There has been damage to some of the private homes and also to the hotels ... particularly those on the waterfront on the western and southern part of the island," he told Reuters. "We've had a lot of downed trees, some of the large trees."
King said he expected power to be restored by Tuesday and predicted no long-term impact on the island's tourist trade.
Cuban authorities reported no deaths from the storm, but said it had damaged or destroyed 29,000 homes and caused widespread damage to crops including sugar cane, citrus fruits and bananas.
The central province of Cienfuegos was the worst hit, with about 2,000 homes destroyed and damage to crops including vegetables and coffee.
